entities.summary:
Sir Andrew Trollope (d. 1461) was a preeminent English professional soldier whose career spanned the twilight years of the Hundred Years' War and the brutal opening phase of the Wars of the Roses, making him a pivotal, if morally ambiguous, figure in the transition of English military practice. Renowned for his tactical acumen and leadership of retinues, Trollope served under several prominent commanders, including John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, and later became a key, albeit mercurial, participant in the dynastic struggles between the Houses of Lancaster and York, often switching allegiances based on perceived advantage or necessity.

Trollope first gained notoriety during the final campaigns of the Hundred Years' War, notably at the Siege of Calais in 1459, where he was instrumental in defending the English Pale against French incursions. His tactical brilliance shone during the early Wars of the Roses, particularly at the Battle of Wakefield in December 1460, where his command of a Lancastrian vanguard contributed significantly to the decisive defeat and death of Richard, Duke of York. He continued to play a crucial role for the Lancastrians at the Second Battle of St Albans in February 1461, successfully employing innovative defensive tactics against the Yorkist forces of the Earl of Warwick. His military expertise was widely recognized, even by his enemies, who frequently sought to lure him to their side.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Andrew Trollope was a highly skilled professional soldier whose tactical prowess directly influenced the outcomes of several major battles, including Wakefield and Second St Albans, during the tumultuous early years of the Wars of the Roses. His career exemplifies the changing nature of military service and loyalty in 15th-century England, leaving a notable mark on a critical period of English history.
